# 11. Offscreen layers

```lua
local layer, err = ctx.layers:create(w, h)
layer.width, layer.height
layer:draw(function(g) end)
g:image(layer, x, y, opts)
layer:release()
```

`w` and `h` are integers from 1 to `max(ctx.screen.width, ctx.screen.height)`. The buffer holds `w * h` pixels; each pixel is a `gray_levels` color plus 1 bit of transparency. A new layer is fully transparent. At most 4 layers can exist at once; creating a 5th returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. Insufficient memory returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`.

`draw` calls the function immediately and passes it the layer's canvas. The origin is the top-left corner of the layer, and every drawing call from sections 6 and 7 is available. Drawing goes directly into the buffer and does not count toward the per-frame command limit. You can call `draw` from any callback to prepare content ahead of time. It cannot be nested: calling it from another `draw` or from `on_draw` returns `nil, "busy"`. An error inside the function propagates unchanged, and the buffer keeps the pixels it had before the call. On success, it returns nothing.

`release` returns true and can be called repeatedly. After that, `draw` and any `g:image` that uses the layer as its source return `nil, "invalid_handle"`.

Use `g:image` to draw the layer back onto the screen or onto another layer. A layer carries its own transparency: a new layer is fully transparent, drawn pixels become opaque, and `g:clear(color)` makes the whole layer that color, fully opaque.
entries.example:
local layer, err = ctx.layers:create(w, h)
layer.width, layer.height
layer:draw(function(g) end)
g:image(layer, x, y, opts)
layer:release()

entries.content:
# 12. Clock, log, and memory

```lua
ctx.clock:millis()
local t = ctx.clock:now()
ctx.log:info(msg)  ctx.log:warn(msg)  ctx.log:error(msg)
ctx.gc:collect()
ctx.gc:count()
```

`millis` returns the number of milliseconds since the current boot, in the range `0..2147483647`. It wraps back to 0 after about 24.8 days. Compute the interval between two readings as `(later - earlier) & 0x7FFFFFFF`, which remains correct across the wrap.

`now` returns a read-only table. Multiple calls within the same callback return the same snapshot.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `valid` | Whether the time may be shown to the user |
| `year` `month` `day` | Gregorian date. Month 1–12, day 1–31 |
| `hour` `minute` `second` | 0–23, 0–59, 0–59 |
| `weekday` | 0 is Sunday |
| `hour12` | Whether the system displays time in 12-hour format. Does not affect `hour` |
| `date_order` | 2.5: the system date order, `"ymd"`, `"mdy"`, or `"dmy"` |
| `date_sep` | 2.5: the system date separator, `"/"` or `"-"` |
| `offset_minutes` | Offset from UTC in minutes, including daylight saving time |
| `epoch_sec` | UTC Unix time in seconds. nil when it does not fit in a 32-bit integer (after 2038-01-19) |
| `local_sec` | `epoch_sec + offset_minutes * 60`. nil when out of range |
| `revision` | Increments when the time is reset, or when the time zone, the 12/24-hour setting, or the date format (2.5) changes. 1 at the start of the session |

When `valid` is false, the date, the time of day, `weekday`, `epoch_sec`, and `local_sec` are nil. `valid`, `hour12`, `offset_minutes`, and `revision` always have a value; since 2.5, so do `date_order` and `date_sep`.

Order displayed dates according to the user's setting; do not infer the order from `locale`:

```lua
local t = ctx.clock:now()
local parts = { y = t.year, m = string.format("%02d", t.month), d = string.format("%02d", t.day) }
local o = t.date_order or "ymd"   -- hosts before 2.5 do not have this field
local s = parts[o:sub(1, 1)] .. (t.date_sep or "/") .. parts[o:sub(2, 2)] .. (t.date_sep or "/") .. parts[o:sub(3, 3)]
```

There is no event for time changes. Each time a clock face wakes, it compares `revision` and realigns if the value has changed. To align to the next minute, call `ctx:after((60 - t.second) * 1000, fn)`, and call `now()` again after waking, because waking can be delayed by a few hundred milliseconds.

The three `log` methods take one string and return nothing; a non-string argument raises a Lua error. Log lines may be dropped when space runs out; this is not reported as an error.

`collect` runs one full garbage collection. `count` returns the number of bytes the script heap currently uses.
entries.example:
ctx.clock:millis()
local t = ctx.clock:now()
ctx.log:info(msg)  ctx.log:warn(msg)  ctx.log:error(msg)
ctx.gc:collect()
ctx.gc:count()

entries.content:
# 13. Device status

```lua
local b = ctx.device:battery()   -- { percent, charging }
local r = ctx.device:radios()    -- { wifi_on, wifi_connected, bluetooth_on }
local d = ctx.device:display()   -- { dark } (2.12)
ctx.device:keep_awake(ms)        -- postpone idle auto power-off (2.18)
```

No permission is required. `percent` is an integer from 0–100, or -1 if it cannot be read. `charging` is a boolean, or false if it cannot be read. All three fields of `radios` are booleans.

Since 2.1, `battery()` also has `voltage_mv` (battery voltage in millivolts) and `temperature_c` (battery temperature in degrees Celsius, as an integer), which are nil if they cannot be read. When the `net` permission is declared and Wi-Fi is connected, `radios()` also has `wifi_ssid` (the network name) and `wifi_signal` (signal strength, 0–4 bars); they are nil when Wi-Fi is not connected.

## Display status (2.12)

`ctx.device:display()` returns `{ dark = true | false }`. It requires no permission, can be called in both the main session and the lock-screen session, and returns a new table on each call.

When `dark` is `true`, the system dark mode is on: when compositing, the host inverts the **whole frame** before sending it to the screen, including the app's own content. It is `false` if it cannot be read or if the device has no dark mode. After dark mode changes, the host makes the app draw another frame, and that frame's `on_draw` reads the new value. The app does not need to listen for changes (this also applies to apps that use `set_tick(0)`). Dark mode is turned on or off by the system setting, a double-click of the Home key (section 4), and night mode (section 24). It can change at any time while the app is running, and the app receives no event, so read it again in every `on_draw` and do not cache it.

To keep some content unchanged on screen (such as QR codes or barcodes, which cannot be scanned after inversion), draw it inverted when `dark` is true. After the system inverts the frame, the content appears unchanged on screen:

```lua
local dark = ctx.device:display().dark
g:image(code, x, y, { invert = dark })   -- black-and-white image; when dark, draw it as black background with white code, which becomes white background with black code after on-screen inversion
```

Codes you draw yourself follow the same rule: when `dark` is true, draw white bars on a black background. Content that should follow dark mode needs no extra handling. The host provides no switch for "this app is unaffected by dark mode".

## Keep awake (2.18)

`ctx.device:keep_awake(ms)`: for `ms` milliseconds from the moment of the call, the system does not power off automatically because of inactivity. Use it for apps that are in use while nobody touches the screen, such as timers, dashboards, recipe steps and demos. No permission is required.

- `ms` is an integer from 0 to 14400000 (4 hours); 0 cancels. A new call restarts the period from the moment of that call and replaces the previous value; periods do not add up. For longer periods, call it again shortly before it expires.
- It only postpones, never brings forward: when `ms` is shorter than the system's remaining idle time, the device does not power off any earlier.
- When the period expires or is cancelled with 0, the host counts that moment as a user action: the device powers off automatically only after the system's auto power-off time passes with no key press or touch.
- It only prevents idle auto power-off. Locking or powering off with the power key works as usual; it does not prevent power-off when the battery is below 5% and not charging (the same check as section 15).
- It applies only to the current session. When the session ends (exit, return to the home screen, opening a system settings page, entering the lock screen, power-off, an error), it stops at once, and a period that has not expired is also counted as a user action at that moment; the next time the app opens, it starts without keep-awake. While a system screen covers the app (`on_pause`, section 2), the keep-awake state does not change.
- Returns nothing on success. Returns `nil, "invalid_argument"` when the number is out of range or not an integer; raises a Lua error when it is not a number (section 0). Returns `nil, "inactive"` in the lock-screen session: the system sleeps and wakes the lock screen at intervals (section 15).

The device stays awake throughout the keep-awake period and uses more power than with auto power-off; apps that keep renewing it should say so in their description.

```lua
local function start(ctx, minutes)
  ctx.state.pomo_end = ctx.clock:now().epoch_sec + minutes * 60
  ctx.device:keep_awake(minutes * 60 * 1000 + 60000)   -- one extra minute to see "time is up"
end

local function stop(ctx)
  ctx.state.pomo_end = nil
  ctx.device:keep_awake(0)
end
```

The end time is kept in `ctx.state` (section 28), so after the user locks with the power key and comes back, the app can still continue counting.

# 14. Networking

Requires the `net` permission. When it is not declared, `ctx.net` is nil. It is also nil in a lock-screen session.

```lua
local job, err = ctx.net:request({
  url = "https://example.com/api",
  method = "POST",                 -- default "GET"; the available methods are listed below
  headers = { ["content-type"] = "application/json" },
  body = ctx.json:encode({ q = 1 }),
  timeout_ms = 30000,              -- optional (2.18)
}, function(ctx, res)
  if res.ok and res.status == 200 then
    data = ctx.json:decode(res.body)
    ctx:invalidate()
  end
end)
job:cancel()
```

**Request.**

- `url` starts with `http://` or `https://` and is at most 1024 bytes. The host verifies https against the device's built-in root certificates, so https requests fail (`io_error`) when the clock is not valid.
- `method` is `GET` (the default) or `POST`. Since 2.18 it can also be `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `PROPFIND`, `PROPPATCH`, `MKCOL`, `COPY`, `MOVE` or `REPORT` (the last few are used by WebDAV and CalDAV). It is compared byte for byte and must be uppercase; any other string returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- `body` is a string of at most 65536 bytes and defaults to the empty string. A `GET` or `HEAD` request that sets `body` returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`; every other method may carry a `body`.
- `headers` is a table that maps strings to strings, with at most 16 entries. Each name is ≤ 64 bytes and each value is ≤ 1024 bytes. For methods other than `GET` and `HEAD` that do not set `content-type`, the host uses `text/plain; charset=utf-8`.
- A `HEAD` response has no body: `body` is `""` and `bytes` is 0; the response headers reach the app as usual.
- Redirects are not followed. The app receives a 3xx response as is, and `res.headers.location` holds the target.
- `timeout_ms` (2.18) is optional: an integer from 1000–60000, default 30000. It is the whole deadline, from the call until the response has been received. A value that is not an integer in that range returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Hosts of 2.17 and earlier ignore this field, and the deadline is fixed at 30000 ms.
- If Wi-Fi is off but a network has been saved, the host turns Wi-Fi on and connects. Waiting for Wi-Fi also counts toward the deadline: if Wi-Fi does not connect within the deadline, the request ends with `no_network`; if Wi-Fi connects but the response is still not complete, it ends with `timeout`. For how long Wi-Fi that the host turned on for a request stays on afterwards, see “Keeping Wi-Fi on” below.
- `save` (2.18) is optional and stores the response body as a file; see “Saving to a file” below.

Only one request can be unfinished at a time; another call to `request` returns `nil, "busy"`. After `job:cancel()`, the cancelled request holds its slot until the host finishes aborting it. This usually takes a second or two, and lasts at most until the request's deadline. During that time `request` also returns `nil, "busy"`, so try again later (for example, with `ctx:after`). Invalid arguments return `nil, "invalid_argument"`; out of memory returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`. On success, it returns the request object.

When `ok` is true, `status`, `headers`, `body`, and `bytes` all have values. If https fails and `ctx.clock:now().valid` is false, the clock is usually not set. You can ask the user to go online and sync the time first.

The host calls the **completion function** once as a callback after the request ends. The arguments are `ctx` and the result table:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ok` | true when a complete HTTP response was received (with any status code); false when the script heap cannot hold the body (`err` is `out_of_memory`) |
| `status` | The status code; nil when no response was received |
| `headers` | Response headers, with names in lowercase. Values of headers with the same name are joined with `, `. At most 32 entries and 4096 bytes in total |
| `body` | The response body; at most 131072 bytes are kept |
| `bytes` | The total size of the body in bytes, including any truncated part |
| `saved` | 2.18: set when `save` is given — true when the file was replaced, otherwise false; nil when `save` is not given |
| `err` | See the table below |

| `err` | When |
| --- | --- |
| nil | Success |
| `no_network` | No Wi-Fi network is saved, or Wi-Fi did not connect within the deadline |
| `timeout` | Wi-Fi connected, but the response was not complete within the deadline from the call |
| `io_error` | The connection dropped, DNS or TLS failed, or the host cannot start a request right now; with `save`, also a failure to write the file |
| `limit_exceeded` | The body exceeded 131072 bytes and was truncated; with `save`, the body exceeded the save limit or quota. `ok` is still true |
| `out_of_memory` | The response was received, but the script heap cannot hold the body. `ok` is false, `body` is nil; `status`, `headers` and `bytes` are set as usual |

`job:cancel()` cancels an unfinished request and returns nothing; the completion function is then not called. It has no effect on a request that has already ended. When the session ends, unfinished requests are cancelled automatically.

## Saving to a file (2.18)

```lua
ctx.net:request({
  url = "https://example.com/books/three-body.txt",
  save = { to = "files", name = "three-body.txt" },
  timeout_ms = 60000,
}, function(ctx, res)
  if res.saved then
    local head = ctx.files:read("three-body.txt", 0, 4096)
  end
end)
```

When the response is large and the app only needs to store it and read it in parts, set `save = { to = ..., name = ... }`. The host writes the body straight into the file instead of putting it in `res.body`.

- `to = "storage"`: stored as a private file of section 9, with names following the rules of section 9. The body is at most 262144 bytes and counts toward the quota of section 9.
- `to = "files"`: stored as an app file of section 29, with names following the rules of section 29. The body is at most 8388608 bytes (8 MB); the folder is created if it does not exist, and a new file counts toward the 512-file quota. Read it in parts afterwards with `ctx.files:read(name, offset, len)`.
- The file is replaced only when the status code is 2xx and the body was received completely; the host replaces it before calling the completion function. The replacement is whole: after a power loss or a failure, a read sees either the complete old file or the complete new one, as with `write`.
- When the status code is not 2xx, the file is left alone and the body goes to `res.body` as usual (at most 131072 bytes), so the error message can be read.
- Cancelling the request or ending the session leaves the file unchanged.
- A `save` that is not a table, a `to` that is not one of these two values, or an invalid name returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.

| Case | `ok` | `saved` | `body` | `err` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2xx, stored | true | true | `""` | nil |
| Not 2xx | true | false | The body, at most 131072 bytes | As without `save` |
| 2xx, body over the limit, or it would exceed the quota | true | false | `""` | `limit_exceeded` |
| 2xx, write failed, no storage card, or the card is full | true | false | `""` | `io_error` |
| No complete response | false | false | nil | `no_network`, `timeout`, `io_error` |

`bytes` is always the total size of the body. Hosts of 2.17 and earlier ignore `save`: the body still goes to `res.body` and `saved` is nil. When the package declares a version below 2.18, check `ctx.api.minor` first.

## Keeping Wi-Fi on (2.4)

```lua
ctx.net:keep_wifi(ms)
```

If the user has turned Wi-Fi off in the system, the host turns it on for a request (see “Request” above). Turning Wi-Fi on, connecting, and obtaining an address usually take several seconds, so the host does not turn Wi-Fi off as soon as the request ends. Instead, it keeps Wi-Fi on for a while:

- This setting applies only to Wi-Fi that the host turned on for a request. If the user turned Wi-Fi on, it stays on regardless of this setting.
- After the last request ends (it completes or `job:cancel()` is called), Wi-Fi stays on for `ms` milliseconds. Requests made during that time use the existing connection, and the timer restarts when each one ends. If no new request arrives before the time runs out, the host turns Wi-Fi off.
- `ms` is an integer from -1 to 2147483647 (`math.maxinteger`, about 24.8 days). The default is 300000 (5 minutes). 0 turns Wi-Fi off as soon as a request ends. -1 keeps it on until the session ends, for as long as the app is open. Each session starts with the default.
- Keeping starts only with the first request: calling `keep_wifi` does not turn Wi-Fi on. To connect as soon as the app opens, make the first request in `on_load`.
- A new value takes effect immediately, and the time still counts from the end of the last request. If you lower the value while Wi-Fi is being kept and the new duration has already passed, Wi-Fi turns off within about 1 second. If you change it to -1 while Wi-Fi is being kept, Wi-Fi no longer turns off.
- When the session ends (the app exits, the lock screen starts, or the device powers off), Wi-Fi turns off immediately without waiting for the remaining time.
- On success, it returns nothing. If `ms` is a number but not an integer in this range (such as -2 or 1.5), it returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. If it is not a number (a string, or missing), it raises a Lua error.

A host that implements 2.4 keeps Wi-Fi on for 5 minutes by default for every 2.x package. A host of 2.3 or earlier does not have this function: it turns Wi-Fi off as soon as a request ends, and the next request connects again. A package that declares `"2.3"` or lower should first check that `ctx.net.keep_wifi` exists.

### Choosing how long to keep it

The longer Wi-Fi stays on, the faster consecutive requests are, and the more power Wi-Fi uses (with Wi-Fi on, the whole device draws several times as much power as with Wi-Fi off, and battery life is reduced accordingly). Choose based on how the app uses the network:

| How the app uses the network | What to write | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fetches data once when it opens and does not go online again (a daily poem, a one-time weather check) | `keep_wifi(0)` | Turns off as soon as the fetch is done; uses the least power |
| Requests only when the user acts (loading on page turn, search, tap to refresh) | Nothing; the default is 5 minutes | Consecutive user actions do not wait for a reconnect |
| Polls at an interval under 5 minutes (LAN sensors, server status, every 10–60 seconds) | Nothing; to save power, set it to about “interval × 2”, for example `keep_wifi(90000)` for polling every 40 seconds | The keep time must exceed the interval plus the time the request itself takes; otherwise every round reconnects |
| Polls every 5 to 30 minutes | `keep_wifi(interval + 60000)` | The 5-minute default is too short, so every round would spend several seconds reconnecting |
| Polls at intervals over 30 minutes | Your choice: if power use matters, write nothing or `keep_wifi(0)`; if every request should be fast, write `keep_wifi(interval + 60000)` or `-1` | With long intervals, a few seconds of reconnecting each round is usually acceptable, and keeping Wi-Fi on uses more power |
| Must stay online the whole time the app is open (live dashboards, remote controls, LAN chat, continuous reporting) | `keep_wifi(-1)`, and make the first request in `on_load` | The network stays connected while the app is open and turns off only when the app exits or the device locks |

The interval is the time from the end of one request to the start of the next. If the keep time is shorter than the interval, every round waits for Wi-Fi to reconnect, and the user sees requests that are “slow and laggy”.

Example: query a server on the LAN every 40 seconds.

```lua
local POLL_MS = 40000
local status

local function poll(ctx)
  local job = ctx.net:request({ url = "http://192.168.1.20:8080/status" }, function(ctx, res)
    if res.ok and res.status == 200 then
      status = ctx.json:decode(res.body)
      ctx:invalidate()
    end
    ctx:after(POLL_MS, poll)        -- wait 40 seconds after the previous one ends
  end)
  if not job then
    ctx:after(1000, poll)           -- busy and the like: try again shortly
  end
end

function on_load(ctx)
  if ctx.net.keep_wifi then         -- not on hosts of 2.3 or earlier
    ctx.net:keep_wifi(POLL_MS * 2 + 10000)
  end
  poll(ctx)
end
```

- Schedule the next round with `ctx:after` in the completion function, not with a fixed-period timer. This way, slow requests do not pile up (only one request can run at a time).
- `keep_wifi(-1)` suits apps that the user actively watches or that stay plugged in. Ordinary apps should use a specific number of milliseconds, so that Wi-Fi turns off by itself when the user leaves the device unattended.
- Poll only while the app is in the foreground. Entering the lock screen or exiting the app ends the session and turns Wi-Fi off; the next time the app opens, polling starts over.

## Connection reuse (2.6)

A host that implements 2.6 keeps the connection open after a request ends. The next request to the same origin (same scheme, host, and port) reuses that connection instead of setting up TCP and TLS again. On a LAN, back-to-back requests usually drop from a few hundred milliseconds to a few tens of milliseconds, and https saves more. This is host behavior: the interface and results do not change, and 2.0–2.5 packages also benefit.

- If the server closes a kept connection, or the connection goes stale after idling too long, the host reconnects automatically and resends the request once: `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `PROPFIND` and `REPORT` only read and can be resent; other methods are resent only if the request had not been sent yet, so the server never receives them twice.
- If the app sets `connection: close`, the connection closes when that request ends.
- All kept connections close when the session ends or Wi-Fi turns off.

## WebSocket (2.6)

```lua
local ws, err = ctx.net:websocket({
  url = "wss://game.example.com/room/42",
  headers = { authorization = "Bearer ..." },
}, {
  on_open = function(ctx, ws)
    ws:send(ctx.json:encode({ type = "join" }))
  end,
  on_message = function(ctx, ws, data, binary)
    local msg = ctx.json:decode(data)
    ctx:invalidate()
  end,
  on_close = function(ctx, ws, code, reason, err)
    -- the connection ended; err is nil for a normal close
  end,
})
ws:send("hello")
ws:close()
```

A WebSocket is a persistent two-way connection. Once it is open, the server and the app can each send messages at any time, without a new request for each message. It suits matches, chat, live dashboards, and other apps that need to know immediately when the other side acts. To fetch data occasionally, use `request` above.

**Connecting.**

- `url` starts with `ws://` or `wss://` and is at most 1024 bytes. Like https, `wss` is verified against the device's built-in root certificates and fails when the clock is not valid.
- `headers` follows the same rules as `request` (at most 16 entries, names ≤ 64 bytes, values ≤ 1024 bytes). The host fills in `host`, `upgrade`, `connection`, and names that start with `sec-websocket-`. If the app sets any of them, the call returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- `protocol` is optional. It is a subprotocol name string of 1–64 bytes that contains only letters, digits, and `-_.`. If the server does not accept it, the handshake fails.
- The second argument is the callback table. `on_message` is required; `on_open` and `on_close` are optional. Passing any other type raises a Lua error.
- Only one connection can exist at a time. While a connection has not ended (including while it is closing), another call to `websocket` returns `nil, "busy"`. You can open a new connection immediately inside `on_close`. Invalid arguments return `nil, "invalid_argument"`. On success, it returns the connection object, which is not connected yet.
- Wi-Fi turns on automatically, as for `request`. If the handshake does not complete within 30000 ms of the call, the connection ends: with `no_network` if Wi-Fi did not connect, with `timeout` if it timed out after Wi-Fi connected, and with `io_error` if DNS or TLS failed or the server refused the upgrade (answered with a status other than 101).

**Callbacks** are callbacks as defined in section 2, with a 1000 ms limit:

| Callback | When |
| --- | --- |
| `on_open(ctx, ws)` | The handshake completed, and messages can be sent. Called at most once per connection |
| `on_message(ctx, ws, data, binary)` | A complete message arrived. `data` is a string. `binary` is true for a binary frame and false for a text frame (the host does not check that text is valid UTF-8). Fragmented messages are reassembled before they reach the app |
| `on_close(ctx, ws, code, reason, err)` | The connection ended. Called exactly once per connection; no further callbacks for this connection follow |

`on_close` parameters:

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `code` | The close code, an integer. If the other side or the app sent a close frame, this is that frame's code (1005 if the frame has no code). If the connection did not close normally (network lost, timeout, handshake failure), it is 1006 |
| `reason` | The close reason string, which can be empty |
| `err` | nil if both sides closed normally; otherwise, see the table below |

| `err` | When |
| --- | --- |
| `no_network` | No Wi-Fi network is saved, or Wi-Fi did not connect within 30000 ms |
| `timeout` | The handshake passed its deadline, or no data arrived from the other side for 45000 ms while connected |
| `io_error` | DNS or TLS failed, the server refused the upgrade, the connection dropped, or Wi-Fi disconnected |
| `limit_exceeded` | The other side sent a message larger than 131072 bytes; the host closes the connection with 1009 |

**Sending.**

```lua
local ok, err = ws:send(data, binary)
```

- `data` is a string of at most 65536 bytes. If `binary` is true, the data is sent as a binary frame; when that argument is omitted or false, it is sent as a text frame.
- The message is queued and the call returns true immediately, without waiting for the other side to receive it. The host sends messages in call order.
- Before `on_open`, it returns `nil, "inactive"`. After the connection has ended or `ws:close` has been called, it returns `nil, "invalid_handle"`. For data over 65536 bytes, it returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. When more than 16 messages, or more than 131072 bytes in total, are queued and not yet sent, it returns `nil, "busy"`.

**Closing.**

```lua
ws:close(code, reason)
```

- `code` is optional: 1000 (the default) or 3000–4999. `reason` is optional and at most 123 bytes. Out-of-range values return `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- The host sends a close frame and waits up to 5000 ms for the other side to respond. It then disconnects and calls `on_close` (`code` is the code the app passed, and `err` is nil). If you call it before the connection is open, the host abandons the connection; `on_close` then receives `code` 1006 and `err` nil.
- On success, it returns nothing. It has no effect on a connection that has already ended or is closing.

**What the host handles.**

- Heartbeat: after the connection is idle for 20000 ms, the host sends a ping, and it answers pings from the other side with pongs. Control frames are not passed to the app. If no data (including pongs) arrives from the other side for 45000 ms, the connection is treated as lost, and `err` is `timeout`. Apps do not need to implement their own heartbeat.
- No automatic reconnect: when the connection drops, the host calls `on_close`. The app decides whether and when to reconnect (see "How to build an online game" below).
- While the app is paused (section 2), the connection stays open and the heartbeat continues. Received messages, `on_open`, and `on_close` are queued in order and called one by one after `on_resume`. If messages not yet passed to the app exceed 262144 bytes in total (usually during a pause, though slow callbacks can also cause it), the host closes the connection with 1009, and `err` is `limit_exceeded`.
- When the session ends (the app exits, the lock screen starts, or the device powers off), the host closes the connection with 1001 and does not call `on_close`.
- Wi-Fi: while the connection is open, Wi-Fi that was turned on automatically stays on. After the connection ends, the "keep Wi-Fi" timer starts; a WebSocket ending counts the same as a request ending. While the connection is open, the host may turn off Wi-Fi power saving, which lowers latency but uses more power; see "How to build an online game" below.
- The connection and `request` do not block each other: you can make requests while the connection is open.

## How to build an online game (2.6)

First, choose the connection type based on the game's pace:

| Game | Use | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Turn-based, slow-paced (chess, go, crosswords, a daily puzzle) | `request`, polling every few seconds while waiting for the opponent; or WebSocket | One request per move is enough. Since 2.6, back-to-back requests reuse the connection and take a few tens of milliseconds on a LAN |
| Needs to know immediately what the other side did (card games, draw-and-guess, multiplayer quizzes, chat) | WebSocket | The server pushes messages as soon as it has them; no polling is needed |
| Fast action (shooters, racing, fighting) | Not suitable | An e-ink refresh takes a few hundred milliseconds, so players cannot see changes that fast |

The device uses the same approach as online games on phones and the web: HTTP(S) and WebSocket only, with no raw TCP or UDP. Write the server for the standard WebSocket protocol (if a browser can connect to the server, the device can too).

**Design points.**

- The server decides: the device sends only what it wants to do (play a card, place a stone), and the server rules on it and pushes the result to all players. This makes disconnects, cheating, and simultaneous actions by two players easy to handle.
- Keep messages small and few: use short JSON, with one thing per message. Call `ctx:invalidate()` only when the state changes. You can also draw once after receiving several messages (the e-ink refresh is slower than the network).
- Disconnects will happen: the user locks the screen, moves out of Wi-Fi range, or the server restarts. In `on_close`, reconnect after a few seconds with `ctx:after`, and double the interval after each failure, up to 30–60 seconds. After reconnecting, have the server send the complete current state again; do not assume that nothing happened while the app was disconnected.
- Give every message a sequence number or turn number, and discard stale messages.
- Entering the lock screen or exiting the app closes the connection. The next time the app opens, it reconnects and fetches the state again. To continue the previous match, store the room number in `ctx.state` (section 28).
- Power: while the connection is open, Wi-Fi stays on and power saving may be off, so power use is higher than usual. Call `ws:close()` when the match ends. In the lobby or while waiting for a match, `request` alone may be enough.

Example: connect to a match server and reconnect automatically after a disconnect.

```lua
local URL = "wss://game.example.com/room/"
local state = { seq = 0 }
local conn
local retry_ms = 2000

local function connect(ctx)
  local ws = ctx.net:websocket({ url = URL .. ctx.state.room }, {
    on_open = function(ctx, ws)
      retry_ms = 2000
      ws:send(ctx.json:encode({ type = "hello", seq = state.seq }))
    end,
    on_message = function(ctx, ws, data)
      local msg = ctx.json:decode(data)
      if msg and msg.seq > state.seq then   -- drop old messages
        state = msg
        ctx:invalidate()
      end
    end,
    on_close = function(ctx, ws, code, reason, err)
      conn = nil
      ctx:invalidate()
      if code ~= 1000 then                  -- not a normal end: reconnect after a while
        ctx:after(retry_ms, connect)
        retry_ms = math.min(retry_ms * 2, 60000)
      end
    end,
  })
  if ws then
    conn = ws
  else
    ctx:after(retry_ms, connect)            -- busy and the like: try again later
  end
end

function on_load(ctx)
  ctx.state.room = ctx.state.room or "42"
  connect(ctx)
end

local function play(ctx, move)
  if conn and conn:send(ctx.json:encode({ type = "move", move = move })) then
    return true
  end
  ctx.dialog:toast("Reconnecting")
end
```

- Call `play` from `on_input`. If sending fails (not connected yet, or reconnecting), notify the user and do not change the local state; wait for the server's result.
- When the match ends, the server sends an "end" message, and the app calls `conn:close()` (close code 1000, with no reconnect).

# 15. Lock screen

An app can provide a lock-screen picture that refreshes at an interval while the device is locked (for example, a clock, a calendar, or a to-do list).

While locked, the device is in deep sleep and does not retain memory. Each refresh is therefore a separate short session that loads the lock-screen script, draws one frame, and ends. The main program and the lock screen exchange data only through the files in section 9 and (2.2) `ctx.state` in section 28. A lock-screen session does not save `ctx.state` automatically; if the session changes it, it must call `ctx:save_state()` itself.

## Make this the lock screen

When the manifest has `lockscreen`, `ctx.lockscreen` exists in the main program; otherwise, it is nil:

```lua
ctx.lockscreen:set_default()
ctx.lockscreen:is_default()
ctx.lockscreen:clear_default()            -- 2.8
local ok, err = ctx.lockscreen:set_wallpaper(image)   -- 2.8
ctx.lockscreen:is_wallpaper()             -- 2.8
ctx.lockscreen:clear_wallpaper()          -- 2.9
```

`set_default` returns nothing. After the current callback returns, the host shows the system confirmation dialog. The app receives `on_pause`, then `on_resume`; inside `on_resume`, `is_default` already reflects the user's choice. If the app is already the lock screen, no dialog is shown. The user can switch back in system settings at any time, and the app is not notified. Call `is_default` each time you need the answer.

**The lock screen and the cover are separate (2.9).** The lock screen (`set_default`, or the user's choice in system settings) determines what the lock screen shows when the user is not reading. The cover (`set_wallpaper`) determines only the picture drawn over the book page while reading. The two are saved separately and can coexist. Setting one does not replace the other, and clearing one does not affect the other: the same app can be the lock screen (`is_default` is true) and have a cover (`is_wallpaper` is true) at the same time. On a 2.8 host, the two share one slot, and the one set later replaces the earlier one.

**Giving the lock screen back (2.8).** `clear_default()` returns nothing and shows no dialog. When this app is the lock screen (`is_default`), the system lock screen returns to the user's own choice from before this app took over, and `is_default` is false afterwards. The cover is not affected (2.9; on a 2.8 host, the cover is given back too). When this app is not the lock screen, the call has no effect. Use it for an in-app “stop using as lock screen” switch.

**Clearing the cover (2.9).** `clear_wallpaper()` returns nothing and shows no dialog. When this app has a cover (`is_wallpaper`), the call removes it. Afterwards, `is_wallpaper` is false, and the lock screen no longer draws a picture over the page while reading. The lock screen is not affected. When there is no cover, the call has no effect. Use it for an in-app “stop using as cover” switch.

**Lock-screen wallpaper (2.8).** `set_wallpaper(image)` scales an image (section 8, a package image or a runtime image) or an off-screen layer (section 11) to fill the portrait screen, and saves it as this app's lock-screen wallpaper. The host stores it at the device's gray depth. This picture is a “cover” for reading, and it is drawn only while reading (2.8.4):

- **Reading when the device locks** (the system reader is in the foreground, for EPUB, TXT, XTC, and so on): the picture is drawn over the page being read. Transparent areas show the page, and opaque areas cover it. If the picture has no transparent pixels, the whole picture is shown. If the reader has a menu, table of contents, or popup open, the layer underneath is still the book page, not the menu. In landscape reading, the lock screen stays in landscape: the picture is rotated upright for the reading direction and centered, and any part outside the screen is cropped.
- **Not reading when the device locks** (home, bookshelf, system settings, an Ink App, and so on): the picture is not drawn, and the current lock screen is shown as usual. If this app (or another app) is the lock screen, its lock-screen session runs; otherwise, the user's choice in system settings is shown (default wallpaper, book cover, custom wallpaper, live desktop, and so on).
- Lock-screen previews in system settings and the phone app follow the same rules: while reading, they preview the cover over the page; otherwise, they preview the current lock screen.

While reading, the lock screen draws only the cover: no lock-screen session runs, and there are no timed wakes. To change the picture, call the function again. The device has only one cover at a time: if another app sets a cover, it replaces this app's cover (`is_wallpaper` becomes false). When the user picks a lock screen again on the lock-screen page of system settings, the cover is cleared as well. Changing the lock screen elsewhere (such as “Set as wallpaper” in the image viewer, or the phone app) does not necessarily clear the cover. To check whether the cover is still there, call `is_wallpaper` each time you need the answer.

- If this app is already the lock screen or already has a cover, the change takes effect immediately, and the call returns `true`.
- Otherwise, it returns `true`, and after the current callback returns, the host shows the same system confirmation dialog as for `set_default`. The app receives `on_pause`, then `on_resume`; inside `on_resume`, `is_wallpaper` already reflects the user's choice. If the user declines, the image is discarded. Calling it again before the dialog appears returns `nil, "busy"`.
- Setting a cover does not change `is_default` (2.9; on a 2.8 host, `is_default` is false once the app has the cover). When this app already has a cover, `set_default` makes it the lock screen immediately without a dialog. After the call returns, `is_default` is already true, the cover is kept, and `is_wallpaper` is still true (2.9; on a 2.8 host, `is_wallpaper` becomes false).
- If `image` is not an image or a layer, it returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. If it has already been released, it returns `nil, "invalid_handle"`. If memory runs out, it returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`. If a read or write fails, it returns `nil, "io_error"`.

As with `is_default`, the app is not notified when the user changes the setting in system settings. Call `is_wallpaper` when you need the answer.

## When it runs

The system decides whether and when to lock (on idle timeout or when the power key is pressed). When this app is the lock-screen app:

1. If an app is running in the foreground, its session ends first (`on_leave`).
2. One lock-screen session runs, with `ctx.lock.reason` set to `"first"`.
3. The device sleeps until the next whole multiple of `interval_sec` in local time (an interval of 60 wakes on the minute). If the clock is not valid, it sleeps for `interval_sec` seconds.
4. The device wakes and runs one lock-screen session, with `reason` set to `"timer"`, and then returns to step 3.

A device without timer wakes performs only step 2.

## One lock-screen session

The host calls `on_load(ctx)`, then `on_draw(ctx, g)`, then presents the frame and ends the session. The two callbacks have at most 2000 ms in total, and this cannot be extended. These are the only two callbacks. `ctx:after` and `ctx:set_tick` have no effect, `ctx.budget:extend()` returns `nil, "inactive"`, and `ctx.screen:set_orientation` (2.18) returns `nil, "inactive"`.

The canvas starts as paper color each time, and each session draws a complete frame. By default, `first` uses a full refresh and `timer` uses a partial refresh. Calling `ctx:invalidate("full")` from `on_load` or `on_draw` switches to a full refresh. The host keeps the count of consecutive partial refreshes in a record that survives sleep, and it inserts automatic full refreshes as usual.

In a lock-screen session, `ctx` is the same as in the main program: `require` works as usual, and the screen orientation follows `display.orientation` in the manifest. Only the following differ: `ctx.lock` exists; `ctx.net` and `ctx.lockscreen` are nil; `ctx.input:text` returns `nil, "inactive"`; `ctx:after` and `ctx:set_tick` have no effect; `ctx.budget:extend()` returns `nil, "inactive"`. On a device where `ctx.device.lock_timer` is false, only the `first` session runs.

In a timer-wake session (`reason` is `"timer"`), the host does not turn on Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, regardless of the user's switches: `wifi_on`, `wifi_connected`, and `bluetooth_on` from `ctx.device:radios()` are all false. After the user leaves the lock screen with the power key, the radios return to the user's settings. The `first` session is not affected.

```lua
ctx.lock.reason        -- "first" | "timer"
ctx.lock.elapsed_sec   -- seconds since the previous lock-screen present; 0 for first
ctx.lock.interval_sec  -- the current interval
ctx.lock:set_interval(seconds)
```

`ctx.lock` exists only in a lock-screen session. The argument of `set_interval` is an integer from 30 to 3600. The new interval takes effect from the sleep after the current session, and the function returns nothing. The next time the device enters the lock screen, the interval starts again from the manifest value.

When the clock is not valid, the session still runs. `ctx.clock:now().valid` is false, and the script decides what to draw.

## Exceptions

- If the lock-screen script errors or times out, the host draws the system default lock-screen picture and stops timer wakes until the next time the device enters the lock screen.
- Below 5% battery and not charging: the script does not run. The host draws the low-battery screen and powers off.
- Power key: the device leaves the lock screen and returns to the system. The app that was in the foreground before locking opens again as an entirely new session.
entries.example:
ctx.lockscreen:set_default()
ctx.lockscreen:is_default()
ctx.lockscreen:clear_default()            -- 2.8
local ok, err = ctx.lockscreen:set_wallpaper(image)   -- 2.8
ctx.lockscreen:is_wallpaper()             -- 2.8
ctx.lockscreen:clear_wallpaper()          -- 2.9

# 16. UI library

Optional capability `ui`: when it is true, `ctx.ui` exists. Otherwise it is nil. The library uses immediate mode: on every frame, you declare all controls again inside `on_draw`. The library draws them, hit-tests them, and manages focus.

```lua
local ui = ctx.ui:create()        -- create it once in on_load

function on_draw(ctx, g)
  ui:begin_frame(g)
  ui:label("title", { x = 20, y = 20, w = 440, h = 40, text = "Settings", font = ctx.fonts.large })
  ui:switch("wifi", { x = 20, y = 80, w = 440, h = 56, text = "Wi-Fi", selected = wifi })
  ui:button("save", { x = 20, y = 160, w = 200, h = 56, text = "Save", radius = 8 })
  ui:end_frame()
end

function on_input(ctx, ev)
  local id, action = ui:handle_event(ev)
  if action == "activate" then
    if id == "wifi" then wifi = not wifi end
    ctx:invalidate()
    return true
  end
  if action then ctx:invalidate(); return true end
  return false
end
```

You can omit the `opts` of `ctx.ui:create(opts)`. (2.13) It also accepts `skins`; see “State, skins and custom regions (2.13)”.

`begin_frame` returns `nil, "busy"` when the previous frame had no `end_frame`. `end_frame` returns `nil, "invalid_argument"` when there was no `begin_frame`. The library does not clear the screen. Call `g:clear()` yourself before `begin_frame`. Controls default to `ctx.fonts.medium` and color 15.

Each control's `id` is a non-empty string, and it cannot repeat within a frame (a repeat returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`). `x`, `y`, `w`, and `h` are required. `w` and `h` are at least 1 (2.15: children inside a container can omit them, and `w` and `h` can also be `"fit"` or a percentage; see “Layout (2.15)”). More than 128 controls in one frame, or a container nested more than 16 levels deep, returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`, and that control is not drawn.

| Control | Fields | How it is drawn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `text` `font` `color` `align` `valign` | Drawn in the box as `text_box`, with `overflow` of `ellipsis` |
| `button` | `text` `font` `radius` `image` `border` | A stroked rounded box with centered text. When focus is drawn, the fill is 15 and the text is 0. (2.8) With `border = false`, no stroke is drawn; focus still fills |
| `switch` | `text` `font` `selected` | Text on the left, an `h × h` box on the right, filled when `selected`. When focus is drawn, the stroke is 2. (2.14) Drawn as a capsule, and accepts `note` `skin` `radius`; see “Switch (2.14)” |
| `image` | `source` | An image object scaled to `w × h` |
| `field` (2.9) | `text` `font` `radius` `placeholder` and others | A text field. See “Text fields (2.9)” |
| `region` (2.13) | `draw` | The library draws nothing; the `draw` callback draws it. See “Custom regions” |
| `tabs` `radio` `stepper` `pager` `list` `progress` (2.14) | See “Tabs, radio buttons… (2.14)” | Tabs, radio buttons, stepper, pager, paged list, progress bar |
| `row` `column` | `gap` `children`; (2.15) `padding` `row_gap` `column_gap` `justify_content` `align_items` `align_content` `wrap` `divider`, appearance `border` `line_width` `border_color` `background` `radius` `skin` | See below |
| `grid` (2.15) | `columns` `rows` `auto_rows` `gap` `row_gap` `column_gap` `padding` `justify_content` `align_content` `justify_items` `align_items` `children`, appearance same as above | A grid. See “Layout (2.15)” |
| `stack` (2.15) | `padding` `justify_items` `align_items` `children`, appearance same as above | Overlaid. See “Layout (2.15)” |

`children` of `row` and `column` is an array. Each item is `{ kind = "button", id = "...", w = ..., h = ..., ... }`, without `x` or `y`. A `row` lays out its children left to right from its own `(x, y)`, with tops aligned. A `column` lays them out top to bottom, with left edges aligned. Adjacent children are separated by `gap` (default 0). Content outside the container is clipped. (2.15) A package whose manifest declares 2.15 or later is laid out according to “Layout (2.15)”; content outside the container is still drawn, not clipped.

**Image buttons (2.8)**: a `button`'s `image` is an image object (section 8), scaled to `w × h` to fill the button. With `text`, the text is centered on the image (color 15). When focus is drawn, there is no fill; instead, a 2-pixel frame is drawn 3 pixels outside the button (with `radius`, its corner radius is radius + 3). An `image` that is not an image object, or a `border` that is not a boolean, returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.

```lua
ui:button("feed", { x = 40, y = 600, w = 96, h = 96, image = ctx.package:image("bowl"), border = false })
```

(2.13) `button`, `switch`, `field`, and `region` are collectively called focusable controls, and accept `enabled` and `nav`. `button` also accepts `selected`, `emphasis`, and `skin`. `label` and `button` accept `font_min`. See “State, skins and custom regions (2.13)”. (2.14) `button` also accepts `align`, and `button` and `region` accept `badge`. The parts of a composite control can also receive focus.

**Hit testing**: the last `button`, `switch`, (2.9) `field`, or (2.13) `region` added in this frame that contains the point. (2.13) A disabled control is not hit, and the hit does not pass through to the controls below it.

**Focus**: hittable controls are ordered by when they were added. Focus is kept across frames by `id` and checked at `end_frame`: if that `id` is absent in this frame, focus falls on the first control. If no control is hittable, focus is empty. (2.13) A disabled control is not in the focus order: “the first control” means the first available one. When the kept `id` is disabled in this frame, focus moves to the available control whose center is closest to it; ties go to the control declared first.

You can call `ctx.ui:create()` more than once. Each UI object keeps its own focus, independent of the others; an object whose `begin_frame` is not called keeps its focus unchanged.

`handle_event(ev)` returns `id, action`. When there is no matching action, it returns nil, nil. (2.14) Composite controls also return a third value and have a `change` action; see “Parts and the third return value”:

| Input | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `down` of `ok` | The focused control, `press` |
| `up` of `ok`, and focus did not move | The focused control, `activate` |
| `down` of `up` / `left` | Focus moves to the previous control. `id` is the new focus, `action` is `focus` |
| `down` of `down` / `right` | Focus moves to the next control. Otherwise the same as above |
| (2.13) arrow keys, manifest `api` ≥ 2.13 | Move by position, see “Navigation by position (2.13)”; this replaces the two rows above |
| Pointer `tap` or `double_tap` | The hit control, `activate`. Focus moves to it |
| Pointer `hold` | The hit control, `long_press` |
| (2.9) `activate` on a `field` | Editing starts, `action` is `edit`. See “Text fields (2.9)” |
| (2.14) `activate` on a part of a composite control | When the value changes, `action` is `change`, and the third value is the new value |

An `ev` that is not an event table from section 4 returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. A control does not store `selected`; the script passes it on every frame. The library does not draw a pressed look; `press` only notifies the script, see “Not drawing a pressed look”. (2.13) `handle_event` returns no action for a disabled control.

**Whether focus is drawn**: focus is drawn only while keys drive it. A device without a touchscreen always draws it. A device with a touchscreen starts drawing it after a key event is passed to `handle_event`, and stops drawing it after a pointer event is passed to `handle_event` (the focus itself is kept, and the next key press starts from it).

`double_tap` is the second tap: two quick taps on a button produce two `activate` results, and a switch toggles twice.

## Setting focus (2.7)

```lua
ui:focus(id)          -- no return value
local id = ui:focused()
```

(2.14) `ui:focus(id, part)` and `ui:focused()` return `id, part` for the parts of composite controls; see “Focus of composite controls”.

`focus(id)` replaces the kept focus with `id`. At the next `end_frame`, it is checked like any other kept focus: if this frame has a `button`, `switch`, (2.9) `field`, or (2.13) `region` with that `id`, focus stays on it; if not (or if it is a `label`, `image`, `row`, or `column`), focus falls on the first control. You can call it at any time, including between `begin_frame` and `end_frame`. It draws nothing and puts nothing on screen; to show the new focus, call `ctx:invalidate()` as usual. It does not change whether focus is drawn (see above), and `handle_event` does not return `focus` as a result of it. An empty `id` returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`; a non-string raises a Lua error (section 0).

Until the next `end_frame`, focus is that `id`: `focused()` returns it, and `ok` produces `press` and `activate` for it; arrow keys move among the previous frame's controls, starting from the first control if `id` is not among them. After `invalidate`, the host redraws before the next event (section 5), so calling it together with `invalidate` avoids this case.

`focused()` returns the kept focus `id`, or nil when there is no focus. It returns nil for a newly created object and when the previous frame had no hittable control.

Example: open another screen from a button, and return focus to that button when coming back.

```lua
local screen, back_to = "home", nil

function on_input(ctx, ev)
  if ev.type == "key" and ev.key == "back" and screen ~= "home" then
    if ev.phase == "up" then
      screen = "home"
      ui:focus(back_to)          -- back to the button that opened this screen
      ctx:invalidate()
    end
    return true
  end
  local id, action = ui:handle_event(ev)
  if action == "activate" and screen == "home" then
    back_to, screen = id, id       -- the button id is the screen it opens
    ctx:invalidate()
    return true
  end
  if action then ctx:invalidate(); return true end
  return false
end
```

To return to a position several levels back, the script keeps its own table as a stack: push `focused()` when entering a screen, and pop and call `focus` when leaving it. Also use `focus` to stay on an adjacent item after deleting a list item, or to start on “Cancel” when showing a confirmation.

## Text fields (2.9)

```lua
local todo = { title = "", note = "" }

function on_draw(ctx, g)
  g:clear()
  ui:begin_frame(g)
  ui:field("title", { x = 24, y = 96, w = 432, h = 56, text = todo.title, placeholder = "What to do",
    max_chars = 24, enter = "next",
    on_change = function(ctx, text) todo.title = text; ctx:invalidate() end })
  ui:field("note", { x = 24, y = 168, w = 432, h = 120, text = todo.note, placeholder = "Note",
    multiline = true, max_chars = 200, enter = "done",
    on_change = function(ctx, text) todo.note = text; ctx:invalidate() end,
    on_end = function(ctx) ctx:invalidate() end })
  ui:button("save", { x = 24, y = 304, w = 432, h = 56, text = "Save" })
  ui:end_frame()
end

function on_input(ctx, ev)
  local id, action = ui:handle_event(ev)
  if id == "save" and action == "activate" then
    ui:stop_edit()
    save(ctx, todo)
  end
  if action then ctx:invalidate(); return true end
  return false
end
```

`field` is a hittable control. It joins the focus order by when it was added, together with `button` and `switch`. It edits text with the docked input from section 4. Fields:

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `text` | The current text. The script passes it on every frame; the library does not store it. Default `""` |
| `font` | The font used to draw the text when not editing. Default `ctx.fonts.medium` |
| `radius` | The corner radius of the box |
| `placeholder` `max_chars` `kind` `multiline` `enter` `on_change` `on_end` | The same as in `ctx.input:edit`. They are passed to it when editing starts |

**How it is drawn**: a stroked box (line width 1, or 2 when focus is drawn). The box keeps 8 pixels of margin on each side, and `text` is drawn inside. When `kind` is `"secret"`, each character is drawn as `*`. A single line is vertically centered, with an ellipsis when it overflows. Multiple lines wrap by character from top to bottom, and the overflow is clipped. When `text` is empty, `placeholder` is drawn (color 8). While editing, the host redraws the text and the cursor inside the box (section 4, “Text area”).

**Starting to edit**: `activate` on a `field` (a tap, or `ok` while focus is on it) calls `ctx.input:edit` with the fields declared in the previous frame. `rect` is the area inside the box after the margin. `handle_event` returns `id, "edit"`. When editing cannot start (for example `busy`, or a value of `max_chars`, `kind`, and so on that breaks the rules), it returns `id, "activate"` as usual: `ui:field` itself checks only `x`, `y`, `w`, and `h`, and the edit options are checked only when editing starts. A wrong type (such as `multiline = "yes"`) raises a Lua error in `handle_event`. Another `activate` on the `field` being edited does not restart editing, and still returns `id, "edit"`. While editing, a tap inside the box moves the cursor. The host handles the tap and does not pass it to `handle_event`.

**Ending the edit**:

- When editing ends with the confirm key or the back key, the library first calls the field's `on_end`. When `enter` is `"next"` and the key was the confirm key, the library then starts editing the first `field` after it in the previous frame's order, focus moves there, and the keyboard stays up. With no `field` after it, editing ends.
- While editing, `activate` on another `field` of this object ends the current edit (without calling its `on_end`) and starts editing that `field`; the keyboard stays up. If editing cannot start on that `field`, it returns `id, "activate"`, and the original edit has already ended.
- `ui:stop_edit()` ends this object's current edit, hides the keyboard, and returns the final text. It does not call `on_end`. When nothing is being edited, it returns nil.
- At `end_frame`, if the `field` being edited was not declared in this frame, the library ends the edit without calling `on_end`. You do not need to hide the keyboard separately when changing screens.

`ui:editing()` returns the `id` of the `field` this object is editing, or nil when there is none.

Only one of `ctx.input:edit` called by the script and a `field` edit can be active at a time. The other returns `busy`.

## State, skins and custom regions (2.13)

```lua
ui = ctx.ui:create({
  skins = {
    iron = { image = ctx.package:image("iron"), edge = 14, pad = { 8, 12 },
             selected = { image = ctx.package:image("iron_on") } },
  },
})

function on_draw(ctx, g)
  g:clear()
  ui:begin_frame(g)
  ui:button("buy", { x = 24, y = 700, w = 200, h = 64, text = "Buy", skin = "iron",
    enabled = money >= price, font_min = 13 })
  for i = 1, 9 do
    ui:region("bag" .. i, { x = 24 + (i - 1) % 3 * 72, y = 300 + (i - 1) // 3 * 72, w = 64, h = 64,
      selected = pick == i, draw = function(g, r, st) draw_slot(g, r, bag[i], st) end })
  end
  ui:end_frame()
end
```

### Creation options

`ctx.ui:create(opts)`: you can omit `opts`. If it is not a table, or one of the items below breaks the rules, it returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Unknown fields are ignored.

- `skins`: a table that maps names (non-empty strings) to skins. Each skin has these fields:

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `image` | An image object. Required |
| `edge` | The nine-slice edge widths: an integer 0–255, or 1–4 such integers, in CSS order: `{ all }`, `{ top/bottom, left/right }`, `{ top, left/right, bottom }`, `{ top, right, bottom, left }`. Default 0, which stretches the whole image |
| `pad` | The text-area padding, written like `edge`. Defaults to `edge` |
| `text_color` | 0..15, default 15 |
| `focused` `selected` `disabled` `emphasis` | State variants: a table that can set `image`, `edge`, `text_color`; fields not set are taken from this skin |

`left + right` must be less than the image width, and `top + bottom` must be less than the image height. A variant is checked against its own `image` and `edge`.

### New control fields

| Field | Used by | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `button` `switch` `field` `region` | Boolean, default true |
| `selected` | `button` `region` (`switch` already has it) | Boolean, default false |
| `emphasis` | `button` | Boolean, default false. For a guiding or primary button |
| `skin` | `button` | A name registered in `create` |
| `font_min` | `label` `button` | An integer 8–96, the minimum font size. See “Shrinking the font” |
| `nav` | `button` `switch` `field` `region` | `{ up = id, down = id, left = id, right = id }`; you can set only some of them, and the values are strings. See “Navigation by position” |

A wrong type, an unregistered `skin`, or `skin` and `image` set together returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`, and that control is not drawn.

### Disabled

A control with `enabled = false` is not hit (and the hit does not pass through), is not in the focus order, and is skipped by the arrow keys; `handle_event` returns no action for it. By default, it is drawn as usual and then covered with white dots using `g:pattern` (`kind = "dot"`, `density = 50`, `color = 0`); without the `pattern` capability, it is not covered. A `region` is not covered; the script draws it according to `st.enabled`. A disabled `field` cannot start editing.

### Not drawing a pressed look

The library does not draw a pressed look and gives the script no pressed state: a pointer `down` returns no action, there is no `release` action, and a `region`'s `st` and `ui:skin` have no `pressed`. `ok`'s `down` still returns `press`, which only notifies the script.

Rationale: an e-ink screen takes about 0.5 seconds per frame. A light tap lasts about 0.2 seconds from down to up, so the pressed frame has not been refreshed when the finger lifts, and the two frames merge into one refresh. The user never sees the pressed look, but the library draws an extra frame. If the tap arrives during a refresh, two more refreshes are needed, and the result appears 1.4 seconds after the tap. The feedback for a tap is the frame after `activate`. `create` has no `pressed` option (the 2.13 draft had one, removed before release); if you set it, it is ignored as an unknown field.

### How buttons are drawn

States in order of priority: disabled, selected, emphasis, focus, normal.

Without a skin:

| State | How it is drawn |
| --- | --- |
| selected | Fill 15, text 0; when focus is drawn, a 2-pixel frame is also drawn 3 pixels outside the button |
| emphasis | Stroke width 3; when focus is drawn, it fills as usual. (2.14) Changed to fill 15, text 0; when focus is drawn, a 2-pixel frame is also drawn 3 pixels outside the button |
| focus | Unchanged: fill 15, text 0 |
| disabled | Drawn as when not disabled, then covered with white dots |

Image buttons (2.8): when selected, the image is drawn `invert`ed; focus draws the outer frame as usual; when disabled, the button is covered with white dots as usual.

With a skin, the matching variant is used; a variant that is not set is derived as follows:

- `disabled`: the non-disabled look, then white dots.
- `selected`: the normal look, drawn inverted.
- `emphasis`: when not set, it is not used; the next state is drawn instead.
- `focused`: the normal look, then a 2-pixel frame 3 pixels outside the button. A selected or emphasized button with focus also gets this frame around its look.

Nine-slice: the four corners are drawn at their original size, the top and bottom edges stretch only horizontally, the left and right edges stretch only vertically, and the middle stretches in both directions. Drawing uses the `src` of `g:image` (section 6), with at most 9 commands, counted against the limit of 1024 per frame. When the button is narrower than `left + right` (or shorter than `top + bottom`), the two corners shrink proportionally and the middle is not drawn; blocks with a width or height of 0 are not drawn. Text is drawn inside the area after `pad`, centered, on one line, with an ellipsis when it overflows. With a skin, `radius` and `border` have no effect. When the skin's image has already been released, the image is not drawn, but the text is.

### Shrinking the font

`font_min = n`: when the text does not fit, the font size shrinks; when it still does not fit at the minimum size, the text is truncated with an ellipsis.

- Fitting: for `button`, the width of the single line does not exceed the text area; for `label`, all the text fits according to its `align`, `valign`, and default wrapping (`font:layout`'s `consumed` equals the whole text).
- TTF fonts (`font.px` is not nil): sizes start at `font.px - 2` and decrease by 2 each time, with `n` tried last, using the same TTF file at that size (on hosts 2.16 and earlier, this is equivalent to `ctx.fonts:open(font.name, size)`; 2.17 has no `open`, and the host still shrinks the same way). Every size tried counts against the 32 combinations; when a size fails to open, shrinking stops at the previous size.
- System fonts: sizes go down in the order `large`, `medium`, `small`, using only fonts whose line height is smaller than the current one and not less than `n`.
- When the text fits from the start, no shrinking is tried, and the original font is used.

### Custom regions

```lua
ui:region(id, { x, y, w, h, draw = function(g, r, st) end, enabled, selected, nav })
```

Hittable and focusable; the library draws nothing. It can be placed in the `children` of `row` and `column`.

- You can omit `draw`, in which case the region is only a clickable area; a non-function returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- When `end_frame` draws the controls, it calls `draw(g, r, st)` in declaration order: `g` is this frame's canvas; `r` is a new table `{ x, y, w, h }`; `st` is a new table `{ focused, selected, enabled }`, where `focused` means focus is on the region and is drawn.
- An error thrown inside `draw` is thrown from `end_frame`.

`handle_event` returns the same results for it as for a button: `press`, `activate`, `long_press`, `focus`.

## Navigation by position (2.13)

When the manifest's `api` is 2.13 or later, the arrow keys move focus by position. Packages for 2.0–2.12 still move forward and backward in declaration order, but on hosts that implement 2.13 they skip disabled controls.

1. If the current focus has a `nav` entry for this direction, and that `id` is an available focusable control in the previous frame, focus moves to it.
2. Otherwise, candidates are found in this direction: their center is on that side of the current focus's center, and their nearer edge is not before the same edge of the current focus. For example, when you press right, the candidate's center x is greater than the current center x, and the candidate's left edge is not less than the current left edge; other directions work the same way.
3. Candidates are compared in order: one that overlaps the current focus on the other axis wins first; a smaller gap in this direction wins next (when pressing right: `max(0, candidate left - current right)`); a smaller center distance on the other axis wins next; the one declared first wins last.
4. When no candidate is found, focus does not move, nil, nil is returned, and focus does not wrap around.
5. When there is no focus and an arrow key is pressed, focus falls on the first available control and `focus` is returned.

Declaration order only decides the first focus, and where focus falls when the kept focus no longer exists.

## Tabs, radio buttons, stepper, pager, paged list, progress bar, badges and ui:skin (2.14)

```lua
local tab, qty, page, pick = 1, 1, 1, nil

function on_draw(ctx, g)
  g:clear()
  ui:begin_frame(g)
  ui:tabs("cat", { x = 10, y = 52, w = 460, h = 52, items = { "All", "Goods", "Medicine", "Misc" },
    value = tab, gap = 4, skin = "btn" })
  ui:list("goods", { x = 10, y = 120, w = 460, h = 448, row_h = 64, count = #goods, page = page,
    selected = pick, draw = function(g, r, i, st) draw_row(g, r, goods[i], st) end })
  ui:pager("pg", { x = 390, y = 580, w = 78, h = 34, page = page, pages = (#goods + 6) // 7, text = "" })
  ui:stepper("qty", { x = 10, y = 640, w = 200, h = 56, value = qty, min = 1, max = 99 })
  ui:progress("load", { x = 230, y = 656, w = 240, h = 24, value = load / cap, style = "stripe" })
  ui:button("buy", { x = 10, y = 720, w = 460, h = 64, text = "Buy", badge = "3" })
  ui:end_frame()
end

function on_input(ctx, ev)
  local id, action, v = ui:handle_event(ev)
  if action == "change" then
    if id == "cat" then tab, page = v, 1
    elseif id == "goods" or id == "pg" then page = v
    elseif id == "qty" then qty = v end
  elseif action == "activate" and id == "goods" then
    pick = v
  end
  if action then ctx:invalidate(); return true end
  return false
end
```

### Parts and the third return value

`tabs`, `radio`, `stepper`, `pager`, and `list` are composite controls made of several parts: each tab cell, each radio item, the stepper's minus and plus, the pager's previous page and next page, and each row of the list's current page. A part is a hittable, focusable unit, placed in declaration order at the position of its control. `handle_event` returns the control's `id`, and the third value identifies the part:

| Control | Part number |
| --- | --- |
| `tabs` `radio` | The n-th item, from 1 |
| `list` | The row number, i.e. the data item index (not the row within the page), from 1 |
| `stepper` | 1 is minus, 2 is plus |
| `pager` | 1 is previous page, 2 is next page |

The third value of `press`, `activate`, `focus`, and `long_press` is the part number. The new action `change` means the control's value changed; the third value is the new value, and the script updates its own state accordingly:

| Part that is `activate`d | Result |
| --- | --- |
| A `tabs` or `radio` item that is not `value` | `id, "change", item number` |
| The `tabs` or `radio` item that is `value` | `id, "activate", item number` |
| The `stepper`'s minus, plus | `id, "change", new value`: `value` minus or plus `step`, not exceeding `min` or `max` |
| The `pager`'s previous page, next page | `id, "change", page - 1` or `page + 1` |
| A `list` row | `id, "activate", row number` |

The library does not store these values; the script passes them on every frame. If the script does not update the value after receiving `change`, the next frame is still drawn with the old value. A non-composite control's third value is nil.

Within the limit of 128 controls per frame, a composite control itself counts as 1, and each part counts as 1 more (a list counts only the rows of the current page).

### Focus of composite controls

`ui:focused()` returns `id, part number`; when focus is on a non-composite control, it returns only `id`. You can omit the `part` of `ui:focus(id, part)`; when set, it must be a positive integer, otherwise it returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.

Focus keeps "control + part", and is checked at `end_frame` as usual. The following rules also apply:

- When the kept focus is a composite control but no part is set, or that part no longer exists in this frame (for example, the list turned a page), focus falls on the control's default part: for `tabs` and `radio`, the `value` item (the first item when there is no `value`); for `list`, the `selected` row of the page, or the first row when it is not on this page; for `stepper` and `pager`, the first available part. When the default part is unavailable, it is handled like "the kept focus is disabled" (focus moves to the available part or control whose center is closest).
- When a part is unavailable: when the whole control has `enabled = false`, all its parts are unavailable. When the stepper's value equals `min`, minus is unavailable; when it equals `max`, plus is unavailable. When the pager is on page 1, previous page is unavailable; on the last page, next page is unavailable.
- Both navigation by position and movement in declaration order treat each part as a separate control. A composite control does not accept `nav`; another control's `nav` can point to a composite control's `id`, which moves focus to its default part.

**Turning list pages**: when focus is on the last row of the list's current page and you press `down` (in either position or order navigation), and this page is full and more pages follow, it returns `id, "change", page + 1`, and focus moves to the first row of the next page. When focus is on the first row of the page and you press `up`, and `page > 1`, it returns `id, "change", page - 1`, and focus moves to the last row of the previous page. These two cases take priority over navigation by position.

### New controls

Every control requires `x`, `y`, `w`, and `h`, and accepts `enabled` and `skin` (`progress` has no `enabled`). `tabs`, `stepper`, and `pager` also accept `radius` and `border`. With `border = false`, the stroke is not drawn, but the fill still is (as with `button`). A `border` that is not a boolean returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. `items` is an array of 1–64 strings. Any value that violates these rules returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`, and the control is not drawn.

| Control | Fields | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tabs` | `items` `value` `gap` `align` `font` `font_min` | `value` is nil or 1..item count. `gap` is the spacing between cells, default 0. `align` is the text alignment, default `"center"` |
| `radio` | `items` `value` `columns` `gap` `align` `font` `font_min` | Same as above. `columns` is the number of columns, 1..item count, default 1. `align` defaults to `"left"`. For multi-select, use a group of `switch` controls |
| `stepper` | `value` `min` `max` `step` `text` `font` | All integers; `min ≤ value ≤ max`; `step ≥ 1`, default 1. `text` is the label shown in the middle, default `tostring(value)`. `w` is at least `2 × h` |
| `pager` | `page` `pages` `button_w` `text` `font` | All integers; `1 ≤ page ≤ pages`. `button_w` is the width of each of the two buttons, default `h`, at most `w // 2`. `text` defaults to `page .. "/" .. pages`; `""` draws nothing |
| `list` | `count` `row_h` `page` `selected` `draw` | `count ≥ 0`. `row_h ≥ 1` and no greater than `h`. `page ≥ 1`; a page past the last page is treated as the last page. `selected` is nil or a row number. `draw` is optional |
| `progress` | `value` `style` | `value` is a number clamped to 0..1; NaN violates the rules. `style` is `"solid"` (default) or `"stripe"`. Not hittable and not focusable |

**Splitting the cells**: `tabs` lays out n cells horizontally. `radio` arranges them in `columns` columns and `ceil(n / columns)` rows, filled left to right, row by row. For k cells along one direction with total length L and spacing gap, cell j (counting from 0) starts at `j × gap + floor(j × (L − (k − 1) × gap) / k)` and ends at the start of the next cell minus gap. The last cell ends at L.

**List**: each page has `per = h // row_h` rows, and there are `max(1, ceil(count / per))` pages. The current page shows items `(page − 1) × per + 1` through `min(count, page × per)`; row k (counting from 0) occupies `{ x, y + k × row_h, w, row_h }`. `end_frame` calls `draw(g, r, i, st)` for each row in order: `i` is the row number, `r` and `st` are the same as in `region`, and `st.selected` is `i == selected`. When `skin` is set, the skin is drawn on the row first, and then `draw` is called. With neither `skin` nor `draw`, the library draws nothing. An error thrown inside `draw` propagates out of `end_frame`.

### How they are drawn

Without a skin:

| Control | How it is drawn |
| --- | --- |
| `tabs` | Each cell is drawn like a button (stroked; `radius` is allowed). The selected cell is filled with color 15, and its text uses color 0. When focus is drawn, a 2-pixel frame is drawn 3 pixels outside that cell (with no fill, so that it is not confused with the selected state) |
| `radio` | Each cell has a circle on its left with diameter `s = min(cell height, 32)` and stroke width 2; when the cell is selected, a filled circle of diameter `s − 10` is drawn at its center. Text starts at `x + s + 8` and is vertically centered. When focus is drawn, a frame is drawn 3 pixels outside the cell |
| `stepper` | Two `h × h` buttons on the left and right, drawn like buttons (filled when focused; disabled parts are covered with white dots). The buttons show minus and plus signs: a centered horizontal bar `n = max(6, floor(min(width, height) × 9 / 20))` long and 3 wide (the plus sign adds a vertical bar), in the button's text color. `text` is drawn centered in the middle |
| `pager` | Two `button_w × h` buttons on the left and right show `<` and `>` and are drawn like buttons. `text` is drawn centered in the middle |
| `progress` | An outer frame with stroke width 2. Inside, with a 2-pixel margin, the filled width is `floor((w − 4) × value + 0.5)`. `solid` is a solid fill; `stripe` is 45° diagonal stripes: one band 3 pixels wide every 5 pixels, slanting up to the right and clipped to the filled area (moving 1 pixel right for each row up). The bands are drawn with filled `g:polygon`; neighbouring bands are joined along the bottom (or top) edge of the filled area into one polygon of at most 128 points, so the whole bar usually takes only a few commands (about 5 at width 432) instead of one per line |

All text is single-line and is ellipsized on overflow; when `font_min` is set, it is shrunk as described in "Shrinking the font". When the whole control is disabled, it is drawn and then covered with white dots (as with a button).

With a skin: each cell of `tabs` and `radio`, and the two buttons of `stepper` and `pager`, are drawn by the skin rules in "How buttons are drawn", where `selected` indicates whether this cell is `value`. With a skin, `radio` draws no circle, and its text is drawn in the area left after `pad`. Each row of `list` is likewise drawn by the skin rules (`selected` indicates whether this row is `selected`), but no text is drawn. `progress` draws the whole bar with the normal look, then draws the leading part, `floor(w × value + 0.5)` wide, with the selected look (or with the normal look reversed when `selected` is not set).

### Switch (2.14)

Since API 2.14, `switch` is drawn as follows (older apps on new firmware look the same). When the width is greater than 32, a margin `p` of 8 pixels is left on each side; otherwise `p = 0`.

- Capsule: height `th = min(h, 34)` and width `tw = min(w − 2p, 2 × th − 4)`; then `th` becomes `min(th, tw)`. The capsule's right edge is at `x + w − p`, and it is vertically centered. Its radius is `th // 2`, and its stroke width is 2. When `selected`, it is filled, and a paper-colored (0) circle of radius `th // 2 − 5` is cut out on the right; otherwise, it is hollow, and a filled circle of radius `th // 2 − 6` is drawn on the left.
- Text: spans from `x + p` to 12 pixels before the capsule's left edge, on one line, and is ellipsized on overflow. When `note` is set (a string; `""` is the same as omitting it), `text` sits at the bottom of the upper half and `note` at the top of the lower half, using `ctx.fonts.small` in color 10; otherwise, `text` is vertically centered.
- `skin`: the skin is drawn at the capsule position (by the skin rules in "How buttons are drawn", where `selected` means the switch is on), and no circle is drawn.
